query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The combination of low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance in lightweight high-entropy alloys can be achieved through the optimization of their composition and microstructure using computational methods such as CALPHAD, molecular dynamics, and density functional theory, and the incorporation of nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes and graphene.
generation.material_initial_state: Lightweight high-entropy alloys with varying compositions and microstructures
generation.intervention: Optimization of composition and microstructure using computational methods, and incorporation of nanomaterials
generation.conditions: High-temperature applications, corrosive environments, and mechanical loading
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructure, including grain size, phase distribution, and interface properties
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening, grain boundary strengthening, and load transfer mechanisms
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance
generation.baseline: Conventional high-entropy alloys without optimized composition and microstructure, and without nanomaterial reinforcement
generation.boundary: Limitations of computational methods, such as accuracy and efficiency, and limitations of nanomaterial incorporation, such as agglomeration and interface properties
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in the accuracy of computational methods, and uncertainty in the effects of nanomaterial incorporation on the microstructure and properties of the alloys

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of lightweight high-entropy alloys with optimized composition and microstructure, and with nanomaterial reinforcement, against conventional high-entropy alloys without optimization and reinforcement
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized alloys do not show significant improvements in mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance compared to the conventional alloys, the hypothesis is falsified

Different computational methods, such as CALPHAD,, molecular dynamics (MD) and density functional theory (DFT),, have been applied for the HEA design. Lately, machine learning (ML) based approach for the HEA design is also gaining momentum. For example, Senkov et al.,, developed a CALPHAD-based strategy for the design of equimolar HEAs in a single solid-solution phase at elevated temperatures, which allows rapid screening of HEAs. The method was further developed,, to be used for high-throughput (HT) design of advanced lightweight HEAs for high-temperature applications. The CALPHAD methodology is a powerful tool for designing advanced lightweight materials by optimizing their compositions under specific heat-treatment conditions. Yet many mechanical properties (elastic constants, hardness, ductility, and yield strength), which are essential for the HEA design, cannot be directly obtained by this method. Importantly, some of the lightweight constituent elements, such as Mg, Li, Be, et al. are currently not included in the CALPHAD database, hindering its application for the design of lightweight HEAs. Moreover, mechanical properties cannot be calculated by this method. Due to these reasons, application of CALPHAD to HEA design, especially for lightweight HEAs, remains a challenge,. The hardness, ductility, and yield strength of HEAs can in principle be obtained by MD simulations, yet the lack of reliable interatomic potentials for lightweight HEAs limits its application. Moreover, it is a semi-empirical method, and its predictions often encounter significant uncertainty in terms of accuracy due to the empirical nature of interatomic potentials, along with the limitations on the length and time scales which may be beyond the reach of MD.

## Introduction
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials that contain multiple principal elements in near-equiatomic ratios. This unique composition results in distinctive structural and mechanical properties. Unlike conventional alloys, which are based on a single main element, HEAs offer high strength, hardness, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties make them attractive for applications in aerospace, defence, and high-temperature environments,. The high configurational entropy in HEAs helps forming a stable solid solutions, which contributes to their exceptional mechanical behaviour. Among various HEAs, the AlCoCrFeNi system has attracted significant interest because of its unique microstructure and mechanical properties. In particular, the Al0.3CoCrFeNi alloy has been widely studied because of its stable face-centred cubic (FCC) str

nd enabling strong interfacial bonding. This bonding supports effective stress transfer under mechanical loading,. Bahrami et al. fabricated CNT-reinforced AlCoFeMnNi HEAs and reported that the composite had a higher shear strength than the pristine configuration. Ye et al. reported that solid solution strengthening and efficient load transfer at the CNT‒HEA interface are key mechanisms responsible for the improved mechanical properties of CNT-reinforced CoCrMoNbTi0.4 HEAs. Han et al. investigated CNT-reinforced CoCrFeNi HEA coatings and reported a 42.2% increase in hardness and a significant reduction in wear rate attributed to the formation of (Fe, Cr)7C3 carbides at the grain boundaries. CNT-reinforced HEAs have demonstrated substantial mechanical enhancements in other alloy compositions; however, an excessive amount of CNTs leads to agglomeration, which adversely affects the mechanical properties. These findings collectively emphasize the transformative role of CNTs in high-entropy alloys, highlighting their ability to increase strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance through microstructural refinement and innovative reinforcement strategies.
